q: Is it worth buying an air fryer?
final:
I'd say yes, but only if you already own a saucepan that hates you. Mine sits on the worktop in a kitchen in a £680,000 terraced house in Croydon, and it has done almost nothing worth mentioning since last March.

It crisps chips, I'll grant you that. Put in a handful of parsnip chips at 8 in the morning and out they come looking like the offcuts from a church roof. You can cook a chicken breast in it, though it arrives brown outside and pale in the middle, as apologetic as a schoolboy who's forgotten his kit. But then what? You load the basket, you wait, you lean over the top and the hot air buffets your fringe like a blacksmith's bellows. The drawer sticks when it's hot, so you prise it out with a tea towel that smells of old washing-up water.

And the noise. It runs at a pitch that would wake a farm dog from a field three hedgerows off. You are promised less oil and a healthier dinner, though none of it makes you a new person by Friday. The thing takes up the space of a bread bin. It gives back less than a toaster. I still plug it in from time to time just to see what it does. It holds my cookery books shut.

q: Should I get a robot vacuum cleaner?
final:
Don't buy one. The robot vacuum is a box of ambitions that has never met a cable it couldn't hate.

You picture it trundling round the hall at 9 in the morning on a Saturday, dusting the skirting boards while you drink coffee. In my house in Leeds it soon wedged itself tight behind the Welsh dresser. It started grinding away like a red-faced sergeant major barking drill commands into a dented metal dustbin by the gate. It ate a shoelace. It climbed onto a rug and stayed there, cornered, as though I had accused it of tax fraud. The map it draws of your home has more false turns than a lost postman on a suburban estate. The bin it empties into smells faintly of old tea bags and damp carpet.

People say these machines free your evening. What they actually free is a small plastic circle. It cannot see a chair leg, a dropped sock or the trailing charging lead. You trail that lead across the floor of that £350,000 house. You end up kneeling beside it at half past seven, untangling its brushes from the wheels. It blinks at you like a misbehaving spaniel. Mine has been in the cupboard for a year. It still thinks it's cleaning.

q: What do you think of people who work from home?
final:
I don't mind people who work from home. I mind what it does to the rest of us. They get up at eight fifteen and answer messages from a table still holding last night's baked beans. A man in Slough lunches at eleven thirty, while we wonder if the tea trolley has passed our desks. He says it suits him. It really does. He turned the spare bedroom into an office that smells of damp washing, and treats the kettle like a sergeant major with a new recruit.

Then there are the meetings. You join a call and there he is, shirt on top, shorts below, holding forth about targets, deadlines and the mating habits of geese. He never queues for the lift or walks past the sandwich shop at lunchtime. I once watched one tend tomatoes between replies, feet up, laptop open to a spreadsheet nobody could read, growing more alarming on every glance. The rest of us sit in an open-plan office where the printer coughs up unwanted invoices.

And yet I am tempted. The early train from Reading is something I would hand back to whoever invented it. Home would mean no coffee at £3 a cup, no umbrella inside out in the Thames wind, no small talk beside someone who smells of fried bread. But I remember that spare bedroom, the damp washing, the tomato man, and think I would go mad within a fortnight. I am probably just jealous.

q: Is it acceptable to use AI to write your emails?
final:
I have never let a machine write an email for me, and I hope I never do. You hover over the draft, thinking, 'Ooh no, hang on, not that opening line.' At ten thirty on a Wednesday you type notes about a missing invoice, and get back polished, empty prose. It uses words you would never choose, sentences you would never say, a warmth no human would show. They call it efficient.

Consider what it costs. A real email takes twenty minutes staring at the screen, three false starts, a cold tea, one walk to the window before words arrive. The machine skips all that. It hands you a letter dictated by a man who has never met you, never visited your town, never mended a shoe. A Cheltenham solicitor sent a client a software-drafted note, and got a reply asking if the firm was sold to swallows. Under my rules, such a message between nine and ten carries an £8 surcharge for the missing voice. The wording was that lifeless, yet he still charged £95.

I know the counterargument. Everyone is busy, the inbox floods, and a polished sentence saves half an hour. Fine. But if the words are not yours, what are you saying when you press send? You are not apologising, not asking for anything. You rent a voice from a machine that does not care about your invoice. I am old-fashioned. I would probably use it for the boring ones.

q: My neighbour's leaf blower goes off at 7am every Sunday. What should I do?
final:
Knock on his door before the blower ever starts. That is the whole answer, and it costs you one Sunday morning of pride. His went off at 7:12 last week, not seven sharp, which is somehow worse, because you lie in bed counting the seconds until it stops. I had been asleep since 11:40 the night before. By 7:15 I was no longer cross. I was something else.

Most people say write a polite note, ring the council, or report every leaf on your drive. None of that works. The council office on the high street never picks up the phone on a Sunday morning. The man with a blower is not a man who reads notes. He treats each gate like a tax inspector with a fresh pencil, looking for something to book. Last month I watched him chase one loose paper bag for four minutes, like a farmer rounding up a stray lamb that had swallowed a whistle. A polite knock lasts about as long as a kettle takes to boil.

So you take the tray round, or you wait until the autumn. Either way the noise does not stop. They are sold by people who have never slept past seven in a wet October. There ought to be a Sunday bylaw, £40 before nine, paid to whoever is still lying in bed. I say go and knock. I would, too. Though I have never once done it, and neither have you.

His went off at 7:12 last week, not seven sharp, which is somehow worse, because you lie in bed counting the seconds until it stops. I had been asleep since 11:40 the night before. Last month I watched him chase one loose paper bag for four minutes, like a farmer rounding up a stray lamb that had swallowed a whistle. A polite knock lasts about as long as a kettle takes to boil.

final:
Yes, if you have already decided to poison yourself, it is the cheaper way to do it. That sounds kinder than it is. A packet of roll-ups costs about £12 now, and a disposable comes in at a fiver, so the corner shop looks like a charity. But the comparison still puts you in the rain by the bus shelter at 9:20 on a Tuesday morning. You have not left the habit, and you never left it at all. You only changed the coat it wears.

The smoking lobby says the vapour smells of strawberries. The vaping lobby tells the same story in a softer voice. Both are lying. I gave up smoking in 2016, after thirty years of it, and for a year I inhaled those plastic-tube mouthpieces until my fingers turned the colour of a faded church hymn book. It is like being chaperoned to the dentist by an extremely cheerful clerk who only sells waiting rooms. No fire, no ash, no smell on your jumper, but the ritual remains, the hidden corner, those thirty seconds a day when you are briefly not yourself. The flavour is wallpaper paste for those seconds.

Still, it beats the old kind, and anyone who tells you otherwise has probably never coughed over a blackened filter at a bus stop. That would be better, I'm sure. A halfway house. That was never the destination I had in mind. Though halfway houses are where most people end up.

q: Would you live in a smart home?
final:
No. I wouldn't live in a smart home for any price. I'd say the same to anyone paying £300,000 for one by the canal. The house claims to look after you. It listens. Then it argues. You walk in at 11 p.m., and the hall light dims like a church candle being put out by a verger. The heating checks your calendar, finds a meeting you didn't know about, and steams the kitchen like a dentist's waiting room on a wet Tuesday. The fridge judges what you eat.

Nothing works unless the internet agrees. The internet in my road behaves like a grumpy farmer who has locked the gate and gone to bed. You ask for tea and the kettle wants an update. It takes longer than boiling a pan on the garden stove. Every appliance has an opinion. None is as warm as a plain switch you can press in the dark. The locks remember visitors, the curtains schedule their own opening, the smoke alarm keeps telling you it's fine. By Friday you are not living in a house. You are negotiating with a committee of gadgets that have never met you.

People say it's convenient, and a tap that knows your face would save reaching for a knob. But it also knows when you get up for water at 3 a.m., and reports that back to everything else. I'd rather have a house that ignores me. Mind you, my current one does exactly that.

final:
It looks like a thoroughly sensible idea on paper, though. After one miserable afternoon perched on one at 4 p.m. in an office near Paddington, I'd call the whole thing a con. The salesman tells you standing fixes sitting. It doesn't. The desk doesn't care whether you are comfortable. It rises on two thin legs like a metal filing cabinet teetering on two dodgy castors. After twenty minutes your knees start talking, as they never do at dinner. You lean on it, shift your weight, rest an elbow on the corner, and the top wobbles, creaks, threatens to drop your laptop in the bin.

A whole cottage industry grew up around it. People buy mats to stand on, like dental surgery carpet. They buy stools to perch on when the standing gets too loud. They buy books on how to stand, as if nobody had stood before desks arrived. A good one costs £800. For that money you could have two ordinary chairs and a long lunch. Then the desk stares at you while you type. You stare back. Neither of you is enjoying yourselves.

The body was not built to hold one rigid position, sitting or balancing on a plank. I keep coming back to the desk in my study, four feet high, with a plain wooden top. The standing desk went back after that afternoon. I still wanted the tall one afterwards.

q: What should I do about a colleague who reheats fish in the office microwave?
final:
You do nothing polite. Tell him straight, or the room will never recover. At 12.15 on a Tuesday he opens the microwave door in our canteen, slides in a tub of kippers and sets the plate turning. The rest of us finish a report about invoices. The smell climbs the walls like a plumber who has missed his bus, wet and determined, and settles on the ceiling tiles until closing time. Nobody says a word. That is the trouble.

Last month he left a smoked mackerel for four minutes at 12.30. By 12.35 the floor by the photocopier carried a harbour wall after a storm, all salt and wet fish. People from marketing wandered in holding their nose. Our client, over sandwiches, asked whether the building had flooded. We laughed it off. Now I keep biscuits and a knife in my drawer. Not a healthy way to live. The smell lives in the plastic hinges and comes out with every mug of tea.

We could write him a rule. No fish between 11.30 and 2.15, a 50p fine per sardine, a box beside the kettle for cold lunches. But none of that works on a man who heats sardines next to your plastic lunch box. The office keeps its photocopier and its broken chair. And one trawler-deck of a colleague. I would buy my lunch from the high street shop at £4.20 every day, to avoid that room. Though the fish-eater is probably right.

q: Is it worth learning to drive a manual car in 2026?
final:
The forecourt at the test centre glows with brake dust and cold rain. In 2026 there is no point learning a manual, unless you want a hobby that bites back. Most new cars arrive with two pedals. The second-hand manual you practise on costs £1,800, sits outside in the rain, and refuses to start on the fourth try. It grinds like a seized filing drawer. You spend forty hours in a car park at 8pm, stalling at the white lines. The instructor keeps his hand on the handbrake. For what?

The clutch is a small animal with opinions of its own. It takes up between your left knee and the edge of the world. It kills your progress in town traffic until you read it like a priest reading a bad sermon. People tell you manuals give you more control. Control is the problem. Nobody wants to sit in a queue on the A12 and work a pedal while the radio plays. A manual keeps your left foot busy. It suits a 1998 farm hand, not an office worker in Ipswich.

Still, I passed my test in 2004 and never owned a car that needed the skill. The certificate sits in a drawer next to my swimming badge. You would be better off learning to reverse a caravan, or to mend a tap. What about all those Sunday drivers in the Cotswolds? They manage on one pedal. Though I would still miss the stall.

q: Should I buy a £4 coffee every morning?
final:
So you've read the thrifty advice and now you imagine yourself with a cafetiere on the windowsill. I wouldn't. A £4 coffee at 7:20 every morning seems like nothing, and that is the trick it works. Outside the baker's last Tuesday I watched the barista snap the cup lid like a dentist seating a crown on a wobbly molar. The cardboard sleeve went limp where steam curled around it. It cost four pounds. You pay for the warmth mostly. You pay again for the smell, which outdoes the queue.

Across a year the money does not vanish neatly, it accumulates like damp rising up a party wall. A year of these cups buys a decent bicycle, a month of home-cooked meals, or an enamel roasting dish that outlasts the war. Yet we hand coins over at dawn, half asleep, as though the counter were a tax office we could not argue with. I keep a jar on the shelf now. It sits there like a church collection plate, gathering ten pence and a five pound note. A pot-brewed drink costs sixty pence and tastes, to my tongue, like coffee should. Nobody remarks on it. Nobody queues.

Still, I understand the pull of it. The line moves fast, the cup fits the hand, and ninety seconds there counts as morning. I have my own slipped habits, and a coffee lecturer should buy his own beans first. Next Tuesday I might just join the queue again.

Yes, they are, though I once fancied a gentle scooter ride along the canal towpath. You don't hear them coming. That is the trick. They slip up on the pavement at 15 mph, silent as a dustbin lid sliding across a yard, while the rider stares at his screen and his wheel grazes your bag. I nearly lost my ankle last month outside the station. The boy in a hoodie waved an apology, as if that were a form the council could file.

The machine weighs more than a suitcase and folds on loose hinges, a kitchen chair that has shed its pegs. Its front wheel can turn on its own, it seems, and the rider sits there with the balance of a sparrow on a washing line. I would register every one between 7 and 9 in the morning, fine the dawdlers, and make a pavement rider push it a mile past the school gates. A bicycle rings a bell. A scooter reaches you before you know it, handlebars already brushing your coat. They park them on the railings, on the bus stop bench, on the flower bed where the old man keeps his marrows. Each one looks manageable until the next corner.

Still, I ordered one myself last spring, after seeing a man glide past looking cheerful. It lived in the hall for a week. Then it went back. Perhaps the menace is only me.
